title: CAN A PERSON BE SAVED, LOVE JESUS, AND STILL END UP LOST FOREVER?
paragraphs: CAN A PERSON BE SAVED, LOVE JESUS, AND STILL END UP LOST FOREVER?
Jesus Said No One Can Snatch His Sheep Away. Hebrews Warns That Some Can Fall Away. And John Says Some Who Left Were Never Truly His. What Happens When All Three Scriptures Confront the Same Soul?
There is a kind of silence that falls over a Christian's heart when someone who once loved Jesus suddenly says, "I don't believe anymore."
Not someone who merely attended church.
Not someone who only knew how to quote Bible verses.
Someone who prayed with tears in their eyes. Someone who worshiped with their hands lifted. Someone who spoke about the cross as though they had personally stood beneath it.
Someone who once told you, "Jesus changed my life."
And now?
They want nothing to do with Him.
Their Bible sits unopened. Their prayers have stopped. The faith they once defended is now something they question, reject, or even ridicule.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you remember how sincere they seemed.
You remember their testimony.
You remember their tears.
You remember the way they spoke about heaven.
So a question begins to disturb you.
Can someone truly belong to Jesus Christ, receive salvation, and later lose everything by walking away?
Or is something even more unsettling possible?
Were they never truly saved at all?
And then another question quietly rises.
What if that person is me someday?
What if the faith I feel so strongly today grows cold tomorrow?
What if I stumble badly enough?
What if I become exhausted, distracted, deceived, or spiritually numb?
What if I wake up one morning and discover that the Jesus I once pursued has become a stranger to my heart?
This is not merely a theological argument.
For some people, it is the question that keeps them awake at night.
For others, it is the question they refuse to ask because they are terrified of the answer.
And for someone reading this right now, it may be the very question God will use to expose a dangerous false assurance—or bring a frightened, struggling believer back to the security of Christ.
Because the Bible contains three passages that refuse to let us settle for a shallow answer.
Jesus says His sheep will never perish.
Hebrews warns about people who fall away after experiencing extraordinary spiritual privileges.
And John says some who departed from the Christian community revealed that they never truly belonged.
All three are Scripture.
All three must be taken seriously.
And none should be silenced simply because another makes us uncomfortable.
Listen carefully to the words of Jesus.
In John 10:27–29, He declares:

"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand." (KJV)
Read those words again.
"They shall never perish."
Jesus does not say, "I will try to keep them."
He does not say, "They will be secure as long as the enemy is not too powerful."
He does not say, "I will protect them unless the forces of darkness overwhelm My strength."
He says they will never perish.
The Greek text makes His promise especially forceful.
The expression is οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna).
It communicates an emphatic denial: they will certainly never perish, forever.
The double negative οὐ μή is a powerful way of denying a future possibility in this construction.
Jesus is not offering His sheep a fragile hope.
He is announcing the strength of His saving care.
And notice something extraordinary.
He says, "I know them."
Before He speaks about their following Him, He speaks about His knowledge of them.
Their security is not grounded in the perfection of their grip upon Him.
It is grounded in the power of the Shepherd who holds them.
But do not overlook the other words.
"My sheep hear my voice ... and they follow me."
The Greek verbs ἀκούουσιν (akouousin, "they hear") and ἀκολουθοῦσίν (akolouthousin, "they follow") are present-tense forms describing the sheep's characteristic response to their Shepherd.
This does not mean genuine Christians never struggle, stumble, doubt, or disobey.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Thomas struggled to believe the resurrection.
The disciples themselves fled when Jesus was arrested.
Yet the sheep of Christ are not defined by a settled, final rejection of their Shepherd.
They are people who belong to Him and respond to His voice.
This distinction matters.
Because there is a tremendous difference between a sheep that has fallen into a pit and a person who has never belonged to the flock.
And there is a difference between struggling to follow Jesus and deliberately declaring that you want no part of Him.
A wounded sheep still needs its Shepherd.
A wandering sheep still needs to be brought home.
And the Good Shepherd is not indifferent to either.
Remember what Jesus said in Luke 15 about the shepherd who went after the lost sheep until he found it.
He did not celebrate the sheep's wandering.
He went looking for it.
That is the heart of Christ.
But just when we begin to rest comfortably in John 10, another passage confronts us.
And it is impossible to read it thoughtfully without feeling the weight of its warning.

Hebrews 6:4–6 describes people who were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, became partakers of the Holy Ghost, tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come, and then fell away.
The passage says that renewing such people again to repentance is impossible, describing their apostasy in terms of crucifying the Son of God afresh and exposing Him to shame.
These are not casual words.
They are among the most solemn warnings in the New Testament.
The Greek word translated "fall away" is παραπεσόντας (parapesontas), from parapiptō.
In this context, it refers to a grave departure or apostasy, not simply an ordinary moment of weakness.
The author is not describing a believer who became distracted during prayer.
He is not describing someone who struggled with temptation and later repented.
He is not describing a Christian who went through depression, spiritual dryness, or a painful season of unanswered questions.
The warning concerns something far more serious: a decisive turning away from Christ after profound exposure to the realities of the Christian faith.
But here is where faithful Christians have disagreed for centuries.
And we must be careful not to pretend that the debate is easier than Scripture allows.

Some Christians understand Hebrews 6 as a warning that genuine believers can finally abandon Christ and forfeit salvation. They point to the extraordinary descriptions of the people involved, especially their participation in the Holy Spirit.

Others understand the passage as describing people who experienced the blessings and power of the Christian community without ever possessing genuine saving faith. They point out that exposure to spiritual realities does not necessarily prove regeneration.
Still others understand these warnings as one of the means God uses to preserve His people: genuine believers hear the warning, take it seriously, and persevere through God's grace.
These interpretations differ significantly.
They cannot all be correct in exactly the same sense.
But each seeks to account for biblical language that deserves careful attention.
And the author of Hebrews himself gives us an important clue.
Immediately after this severe warning, he says:
"But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak." (Hebrews 6:9, KJV)
Do you see the significance?
The author distinguishes the frightening scenario he has described from the "things that accompany salvation" which he expects to see among his readers.
That observation is especially important to interpretations that distinguish profound spiritual exposure from genuine conversion.
Yet the warning remains real.
It is not a decorative threat.
It is not permission to say, "I once prayed a prayer, so nothing about my life matters anymore."
Hebrews repeatedly calls believers to hold fast to Christ.
Hebrews 3:14 says:
"For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end." (KJV)
The passage does not invite us to purchase salvation through endurance.
It shows how seriously the New Testament treats persevering faith.
And now we come to the third passage.
The one that may be the most unsettling of all.
First John 2:19 says:

"They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us." (KJV)
Imagine hearing that about someone you once considered a brother or sister in Christ.
Someone who knew the songs.
Someone who knew the language.
Someone who served alongside you.
Someone who looked like they belonged.
John says that the departure of certain people revealed something that had been hidden.
Their outward association with the church was not the same as truly belonging to the apostolic fellowship.
In its original context, John is addressing people who departed from the community and were associated with false teaching about Christ.
He is not declaring that every person who changes churches, experiences spiritual confusion, or temporarily stops attending worship was never saved.
That would be a serious misuse of the passage.
But his central warning remains piercing.
It is possible to appear to belong to Christ's people without truly belonging to Christ.
The Greek phrase οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν (ouk ēsan ex hēmōn) means "they were not of us."
And John's explanation is that genuine belonging would have been expressed in continuing with them.
This is the biblical foundation for a sobering distinction.
A person can experience religious excitement without spiritual regeneration.
A person can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
A person can enjoy worship music without worshiping God in spirit and truth.
A person can become deeply involved in ministry while remaining spiritually unconverted.
Jesus Himself warned about people who would call Him "Lord, Lord" and appeal to their religious works, only to hear His devastating declaration:
"I never knew you." (Matthew 7:23, KJV)
Not, "I knew you once, but I forgot you."
"I never knew you."
That statement should make every religious performer uncomfortable.
Because the most dangerous place to be spiritually is not always outside a church building.
Sometimes it is inside one, surrounded by Christian language, applauded for Christian activity, and completely unfamiliar with genuine repentance.
You can know how to behave like a Christian without having surrendered your life to Christ.
You can be admired by a congregation and still be hiding from God.
You can become so skilled at looking spiritually alive that you stop noticing the emptiness within.
And perhaps that is why this question hurts so much.
Because we want salvation to be something we can verify by looking backward at one emotional moment.
One altar call.
One prayer.
One baptism.
One powerful experience.
But the New Testament repeatedly directs our attention to the person and work of Jesus Christ and to the reality of living faith.
Not merely to a memory of religious excitement.
And that brings us to a man whose story should give every struggling Christian reason to keep reading.
His name was Peter.
Peter was not a distant observer of Jesus.
He walked with Him.
He heard His teaching.
He witnessed miracles.
He confessed that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the living God.
And when the pressure became unbearable, Peter denied that he even knew Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine turning and seeing the face of the Savior you had just denied.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter.
Then Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come from embarrassment.
There are tears that come from being caught.
And there are tears that come when a human being realizes how deeply they have betrayed someone they love.
Peter wept bitterly.
But his story did not end beside that fire.
Before Peter ever denied Him, Jesus had already said:
"But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." (Luke 22:32, KJV)
Jesus knew Peter would fall.
He knew the denial was coming.
He knew how ugly that night would become.
And still, He prayed for him.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who had denied his Shepherd was not beyond the Shepherd's restoring grace.
Now listen carefully.
Peter's restoration does not prove that apostasy is harmless.
It does not erase the warnings of Hebrews.
It does not mean that everyone who rejects Christ will necessarily return.
But it proves something precious.
A terrible failure is not automatically the same as final apostasy.
And a believer's darkest chapter does not have to be the final chapter.
Perhaps you need to hear that.
Because you have fallen.
You made promises to God and broke them.
You returned to a sin you thought you had conquered.
You stopped praying because you felt ashamed.
You avoided Scripture because every verse seemed to expose you.
And somewhere in that darkness, you began wondering whether you had crossed a line from which there could be no return.
You read Hebrews 6 and felt your stomach tighten.
You wondered whether your failure meant you were beyond repentance.
But the very warning that should make us take sin seriously must never be twisted into a command for repentant sinners to stay away from Jesus.
Christ says:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (John 6:37, KJV)
That is not a promise to people who boast that they no longer need Him.
It is an invitation of extraordinary comfort to those who come to Him.
If you are grieving over sin, do not turn your grief into a reason to avoid Christ.
Bring it to Him.
If your faith feels weak, do not pretend it is strong.
Cry out as the father in Mark 9:24 did:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." (KJV)
If you have wandered, do not make your wandering your permanent home.
Return.
Not because your tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because your repentance earns the cross.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior of sinners, and His mercy is greater than the false image of a Savior who refuses every broken person who approaches Him.
Yet there is another side to this truth.
And it is dangerous to ignore it.
Imagine someone saying:
"I accepted Jesus when I was twelve. I know I am going to heaven. It doesn't matter that I now reject everything He taught."
They have no desire to repent.
No interest in following Christ.
No concern about their deliberate rebellion.
They treat the grace of God as permission to remain in sin.
And when anyone challenges them, they answer:
"Once saved, always saved."
But that slogan, used carelessly, can become a hiding place for spiritual presumption.

The doctrine commonly called eternal security, in its historic perseverance-of-the-saints form, does not teach that an empty profession of faith guarantees heaven regardless of a person's settled rejection of Christ.
It teaches that those whom God truly saves will be kept by His grace and brought to persevering faith.
And Christians who believe genuine salvation can be forfeited also warn against presumption, emphasizing the necessity of continuing in faith.

Despite their serious disagreement about whether a genuinely regenerate person can finally fall away, both perspectives have biblical reasons to reject the idea that deliberate unbelief should be treated as spiritually safe.
Paul wrote:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." (Romans 6:1–2, KJV)
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves sinners and teaches them to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That does not mean genuine Christians become sinlessly perfect.
First John 1:8 warns against claiming that we have no sin.
And First John 1:9 promises God's faithfulness and justice in forgiving and cleansing those who confess their sins.
But it does mean that we must stop confusing forgiveness with indifference.
Christ did not die so that we could become comfortable with the chains He came to break.
He died and rose again to reconcile us to God and bring us into new life.
So what is the answer?
Can someone truly be saved and later walk away?
Or were they never saved in the first place?
The most responsible answer is that Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture have reached different conclusions about whether genuine salvation can finally be lost.

Those who hold to the perseverance of the saints understand John 10 as teaching that Christ will certainly preserve all who truly belong to Him. They interpret final apostasy as revealing that a person's earlier profession was not genuine saving faith, consistent with their understanding of First John 2:19.

Those who hold to conditional security understand John 10 as a magnificent promise of Christ's protecting power, while maintaining that the warnings against apostasy describe a genuine danger for believers who later abandon faith. They do not see Jesus' promise against being snatched away as necessarily answering every question about a person's own subsequent rejection of Him.
Both positions must wrestle seriously with the entire biblical witness.
Neither should be defended by pretending that the difficult passages do not exist.
And we should be especially cautious about declaring with absolute certainty what was happening inside another person's soul.
We can recognize a person's present confession.
We can observe patterns of life.
We can respond to persistent unbelief and disobedience with biblical seriousness.
But we are not omniscient.
God knows the heart perfectly.
We do not.
Here is what the passages make unmistakably clear.
Jesus is a mighty Savior.
A profession of faith is not the same thing as possessing saving faith.
Apostasy is a dreadful matter, not something to celebrate or dismiss.
And Scripture repeatedly calls people to continue trusting, following, and abiding in Christ.
So perhaps the question that should consume us is not simply:
"Was that person really saved ten years ago?"
Perhaps the more urgent question is:
"Am I trusting Jesus Christ today, or am I trusting a religious memory while refusing His voice?"
Because there is a difference.
A person can spend years arguing about whether salvation can be lost while never seriously examining whether they have come to Christ in repentance and faith.
They can memorize theological terminology while ignoring the Savior those doctrines are meant to honor.
They can become experts at debating assurance and apostasy while slowly becoming strangers to prayer.
And that would be tragic.
Not because theology is unimportant.
Sound doctrine matters deeply.
But sound doctrine should lead us toward Christ, not merely toward winning arguments about Christ.
The purpose of studying eternal security is not to become careless.
The purpose of studying apostasy is not to live in constant terror.
The purpose is to understand God's Word faithfully, to take His warnings seriously, and to rest our hope in the Savior Scripture reveals.
Philippians 2:12–13 holds together two truths that we often try to separate.
Believers are commanded to work out their salvation with fear and trembling.
And the very next verse explains that God is working in them both to will and to do His good pleasure.
Human responsibility.
Divine grace.
Serious obedience.
God's sustaining work.
Not enemies.
Not contradictions to be casually discarded.
Truths that should humble us before the Lord.
And if you are wondering whether your faith is real, do not begin by measuring how emotional you feel.
Emotions change.
Some mornings you wake up with a heart overflowing in worship.
Other mornings you can barely whisper a prayer.
Some seasons are filled with spiritual joy.
Others are marked by grief, confusion, and exhaustion.
The presence of struggle does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
Ask instead whether you are willing to come honestly before Christ.
Do you recognize your need for His mercy?
Are you trusting His death and resurrection rather than your own goodness?
When Scripture exposes sin, are you willing to repent, even when repentance is painful?
Do you desire to know Him, even when your feelings are weak?
Do not turn these questions into a demand for flawless performance.
The ground of salvation is not the quality of your spiritual résumé.
It is Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
And verse 10 immediately teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
We are not saved because we produce good works.
We are saved by grace for a life in which God's transforming work bears fruit.
Fruit does not purchase the tree's life.
It reveals something about the life within.
And even here, we must remember that spiritual growth can be uneven.
A bruised reed is not necessarily a dead one.
A struggling Christian is not necessarily a false Christian.
But a person who deliberately rejects Christ should never be encouraged to find assurance in a past religious experience while remaining unwilling to return to Him.
That would not be love.
It would be spiritual negligence.
And perhaps you are not the person who walked away.
Perhaps you are the one who watched someone leave.
A husband.
A wife.
A son.
A daughter.
A parent.
A friend who once knelt beside you in prayer.
You have replayed their testimony in your mind.
You have wondered whether every tear was false.
You have questioned whether every moment of worship was meaningless.
You have asked God why someone who seemed so close to Him now speaks as though He does not exist.
And perhaps, beneath all those questions, there is grief you have never allowed yourself to express.
You miss the person they used to be.
You miss praying together.
You miss talking about Scripture.
You miss the confidence that you would both continue walking with Christ.
Please hear this.
You do not have to pretend their departure is harmless.
And you do not have to pretend you know the final verdict on their soul.
You can grieve.
You can pray.
You can speak truth with gentleness.
You can refuse to manipulate them while still refusing to abandon the hope that God can bring a wandering person to repentance.
The father in Luke 15 did not call the far country a good place for his son.
But when the son returned, he received him with extraordinary joy.
The parable does not settle every theological dispute about whether salvation can be lost.
It does reveal the astonishing welcome of the father toward the repentant prodigal.
And that matters.
Because someone reading this may have spent years in the far country.
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
You have tried to silence the conviction.
You have buried yourself in distractions.
You have told yourself that the Christian life was only a phase.
You have laughed at the things that once brought you to tears.
But something about the name of Jesus still unsettles you.
Something about the cross still breaks through your defenses.
And maybe, even now, you are tired of running.
Then stop treating your past as a reason to remain away.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
Come to Christ because He is worthy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the crucified and risen Savior.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what you know is destroying your soul.
Seek the fellowship of faithful believers who will teach you Scripture, pray with you, and help you walk in truth.
And if you have never genuinely trusted Christ, do not settle for merely returning to religious activity.
Come to Him for salvation.
Romans 10:9 connects salvation with confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead.
First Corinthians 15:3–4 proclaims that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that you can save yourself by holding on tightly enough.
Not that you can earn eternal life by maintaining a flawless record.
Not that a prayer spoken years ago gives you permission to reject the Lord today.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
He is the Savior.
He is the Shepherd.
He is the One to whom the weary must come.
And He is the One whom every professing believer must take seriously.
Perhaps this article has exposed something you have been hiding.
Perhaps you have been trusting a Christian identity more than Christ Himself.
Perhaps you have been terrified that one failure means God has abandoned you.
Perhaps you have been watching someone you love drift farther from faith, and you have not known how to pray anymore.
Or perhaps you have been caught between two voices.
One telling you that your sin does not matter.
The other telling you that your sin is too great for forgiveness.
Neither voice faithfully represents the full Gospel.
The Gospel tells us that sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
And grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
That is why we cannot make light of apostasy.
And that is why we must never make light of mercy.
Jesus is not a temporary religious accessory.
He is Lord.
He is not merely an emotional experience from your past.
He is the living Savior who calls people to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And whether you have been a Christian for fifty years or you are considering the claims of Christ for the first time, the invitation remains centered on Him.
Not on your reputation.
Not on your spiritual achievements.
Not on the applause of other believers.
On Jesus.
The One who said His sheep hear His voice.
The One who warned against false discipleship.
The One who restored Peter after his denial.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who is worthy of our trust, obedience, worship, and love.
So when the question returns—"Can someone truly be saved and later walk away, or were they never saved?"—remember that Scripture gives us both extraordinary promises and terrifying warnings.
Do not erase either.
Do not use assurance to excuse rebellion.
Do not use warnings to crush the repentant.
Do not declare yourself the final judge of another person's eternal destiny.
And do not spend so much time analyzing someone else's departure that you neglect your own relationship with Christ.
Hear His voice. Trust His grace. Take His warnings seriously. And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because this is not merely a debate about who once stood near the Shepherd.
It is a matter of eternal importance.
And I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Have you ever experienced a season when your faith almost collapsed?
Have you ever walked away from God—or watched someone you love abandon the faith?
Have you ever wondered whether you were truly saved?
You do not have to tell the world every detail of your private struggle.
But your honest response might encourage someone who believes they are the only person fighting this battle.
Your story may remind another reader that repentance is possible and that the mercy of Christ is not a small thing.
Please keep the conversation gracious. Christians who disagree about eternal security can still listen carefully, open their Bibles together, and treat one another with dignity.
And if a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them privately or tagging them if that would be welcome.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
But because sometimes a difficult question becomes the beginning of an honest conversation about Jesus.
And invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the person who has grown spiritually indifferent, and even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
Because we are not here merely to collect religious opinions.
We want people to encounter the truth of God's Word and be pointed toward Jesus Christ.

If these writings have helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to return to prayer, or strengthened you during a difficult season, I also want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because paying money proves that you are saved.
Not because you must support this particular ministry to glorify God.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and salvation is never for sale.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating financially in Paul's ministry.
And Third John 5–8 commends faithful support for those who labor in the truth.
You may choose to make it part of your planned Christian giving, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, your family, and others in need.
But it should never replace faithful participation in your local church or be presented as a mandatory tithe owed to Gospel Warrior.
Your generosity should come from love for Christ, not fear, guilt, or pressure.
The mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
Our only Savior is Jesus Christ.
And that is precisely why every resource, every article, every act of generosity, and every invitation should ultimately point back to Him.
To the cross.
To the empty tomb.
To repentance.
To grace.
To forgiveness.
To the new life that only He can give.
Can someone truly be saved and later walk away?
Christians may continue to wrestle with how the biblical promises and warnings fit together.
But there is something you do not have to postpone until every theological question has been answered.
You can come to Jesus Christ today.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can stop treating yesterday's religious experience as a substitute for today's faith.
You can stop imagining that your weakness makes the Savior unwilling to receive you.
You can open your Bible again.
You can pray again.
You can seek help again.
You can take one honest step toward Christ.
And if you are already walking with Him, you can continue by His grace, not boasting in your own strength but depending upon His.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian is not that we have never fallen.
It is that Jesus Christ died and rose again, and that His saving grace is sufficient for all who truly come to Him.

The most frightening tragedy is not that someone once stumbled on the road of faith—it is that someone might spend a lifetime standing near the cross without ever surrendering to the Savior who hung upon it.
